opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. That work was really formative for me. Before my PhD, I spent time at Georgetown Law's Center on Privacy and Technology, where we studied how police departments across the United States were using face recognition. What struck me most was how little anyone in the chain actually understood about the systems they were relying on. Police departments were buying these tools from vendors and running searches against enormous databases, often including driver's license photos of people who had never done anything wrong. When we asked basic questions like "How accurate is this? Has it been tested on different demographic groups? What happens when it's wrong?", the answers were usually some version of "We don't know" or "The vendor says it works."

That was eye-opening. These are systems that can put someone in front of a detective, or in a lineup, and the people deploying them had essentially no way to reason about their behavior. And honestly, as a technologist, I realized that we in the research community didn't have great answers either. We could report a benchmark accuracy number, but that's very different from understanding why a model does what it does, when it fails, or how it behaves on a population it wasn't evaluated on.

So I came away convinced that policy can only be as good as our scientific understanding of the technology. You can't write a sensible rule about accuracy testing or bias audits if nobody can characterize what these models are actually doing. That pushed me toward wanting to do science on neural networks, not just building bigger and better ones, but asking basic questions about how they learn, what parts of them actually matter, and why they work at all. In a way, the lottery ticket work and a lot of what I've done since grew out of that frustration. I wanted us to treat these systems as objects of study we could actually understand, because the stakes of not understanding them are very real for real people.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty about accuracy and demographic testing, but does not identify the belief that an algorithm cannot see race and therefore cannot be racially biased.

r002.rationale: It does not mention the Seattle Police Department or explain its claim in light of public knowledge of machine learning at the time.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So that work was at Georgetown Law, at the Center on Privacy and Technology, before I started my PhD. We spent about a year looking at how police departments across the country were using face recognition, and the report that came out of it was called "The Perpetual Line-Up." And the thing that really stuck with me was how little anyone in the loop actually understood about what these systems were doing.

You'd have a vendor selling a system to a police department, and the department would ask, reasonably, "how accurate is this?" And the honest answer was that nobody really knew. Not in the setting they were going to use it in. Accuracy on a benchmark of well-lit, frontal mugshots tells you very little about accuracy on a grainy surveillance still of someone who's been pulled into a database of driver's license photos. And it tells you even less about how accuracy breaks down across race or gender, which, as we now know from Joy Buolamwini and others, it very much does.

And what struck me was that this wasn't malice. It was that the people deploying the technology, the people buying it, and frankly in a lot of cases the people building it, were treating it as a black box that worked. There was no real culture of asking "why does this work, when does it fail, and what would I need to measure to know?"

That genuinely changed what I wanted to work on. When I got to MIT, I could have gone in a lot of directions, but I kept coming back to this feeling that the field had gotten extraordinarily good at making things work empirically and had not kept up on the understanding side. We train these enormous networks, they do remarkable things, and if you ask a fairly basic question like "why does this architecture need to be this big" or "what's actually happening in the first few hundred steps of training," the honest answer is often a shrug.

So the lottery ticket work, and a lot of what I've done since, comes out of that. It's a very different domain from face recognition on the surface, but the motivation is the same. If we're going to put these systems in places where they affect people's lives, somebody has to be doing the unglamorous work of figuring out how they actually behave. And I think that work is also just scientifically interesting, which is a nice bonus. But the policy experience is what made me feel like it was urgent rather than just interesting.

astra-6.text:
Working on police use of facial recognition made the stakes of understanding machine learning feel very concrete to me. It’s one thing to talk about a model’s accuracy in the abstract. It’s another when its output might influence an investigation into a real person.

And accuracy alone doesn’t answer all the important questions. What does a match actually mean? Under what conditions does the system fail? How do the people using it interpret the result? You need enough technical understanding to ask those questions, but you also need to understand the institution using the technology.

That made me appreciate how important it is to bridge the technical and policy conversations. If we’re going to make consequential decisions with these systems, we need to be able to explain what they can do, where their limitations are, and what we simply don’t know.

r001.rationale: The response discusses accuracy and limitations generally, but does not identify the belief that facial recognition cannot be racially biased because an algorithm cannot see race.

sol-6.1.text:
Working on police use of facial recognition made the stakes of understanding machine learning very concrete for me. You have a technical system whose output can affect someone’s freedom, but the people using it may not understand what that output actually means or where the system can fail. A possible match can start to look like an authoritative answer, even though those are very different things.

And understanding the model’s accuracy is only part of the problem. You also have to understand how it fits into an investigation, who gets searched, and what opportunities someone has to challenge the result. That experience pushed me to think of machine learning as more than a technical exercise. If we’re going to put these systems into consequential settings, we need to understand their limitations well enough to explain them—and to recognize when we shouldn’t use them.
